audits.question: Check the entry's Hittite/Hattic/Luwian/Hurrian language-versus-ritual layering against a located text or scholarly passage; separate script, language affiliation and a deity's cult provenance.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/anatolia-hittite.md:11 (four-category rule), :55 (Hattic table row), :56 (Hurrian row), :61 (script/corpus bullet), :84 (storm-god names row), :45 (manuscript-chronology bullet)
audits.entry_claim: Hattic is non-Indo-European and not Hittite under another spelling; inherited Hattic cult names and liturgical passages survive inside Hittite textual settings; script (cuneiform vs hieroglyphic) and language affiliation are independent ('Cuneiform Luwian'/'Hieroglyphic Luwian' name corpora through scripts); a deity's cult provenance (e.g. the Hattic storm-god father of Telipinu; Hurrian Teššub aligned with the Hittite storm-god) is separable from court language and script; and no demonstrated genealogical relation between Hattic and a modern Caucasian language is established.
audits.source_citation: Lehmann, Winfred P. and Jonathan Slocum (eds.), Hittite Online, Lesson 2: 'The Telepenus "Vanishing God" Myth (Anatolian mythology)', by Sara E. Kimball and Jonathan Slocum. Linguistics Research Center, University of Texas at Austin.
audits.source_locator: Lesson 2 commentary, first two paragraphs ('Reading and Textual Analysis' section header follows)
audits.source_excerpt: Telepenus, son of the Hattic Stormgod, was a god of agriculture … stories, learned and adapted by the Hittites … played various roles in Hittite religious cult.
audits.retrieval_method: Direct HTTP fetch of the public UT Austin Linguistics Research Center page (FetchURL); full extracted page text read from the saved tool-output file; quotations copied verbatim from the retrieved English text, with Hittite given in romanized transliteration with English interlinear gloss.
audits.basis: The lesson commentary names Telipinu as son of the Hattic Storm-god within Hittite cult use (deity cult provenance distinct from Hittite court language) and dates the copy layer: 'The text exists in several copies, the earliest of which follows the writing conventions of the Middle Hittite period, but is probably a copy of an even earlier version' — supporting the entry's line-45 separation of composition, manuscript and copy date. Its interlinear gloss marks IṢ-BAT as an Akkadogram with the note '# The Hittite reading is ēpta', showing logographic spelling vs spoken language inside one clause. Corroborating retrievals below cover Hattic non-IE status, Hattic liturgical embedding ('the priest is now speaking in Hattic'; CTH 725–745 with Hattic/Hittite bilinguals), cuneiform adopted from Assyrian colonies while three Anatolian languages use it, the Akkadian-version copy of the Telepinus Proclamation, and Hurrian Teshub syncretized with the Hittite storm-god. Inspected medium: English-language university teaching pages; no cuneiform autograph or Hattic-language text read directly.
audits.coupling_implication: Supports the entry's register-separated design transfer (household speech / archive language / ritual quotation / monumental register): a ritual quotation can be in Hattic while the framing instruction is Hittite, and a Sumerogram/Akkadogram does not make the clause Sumerian/Akkadian. Deity function can be aligned across Hattic, Hittite and Hurrian name-traditions without collapsing them into one god, and cult provenance is a separate variable from script and court language for worldbuilding inheritance chains.
audits.limits: Both direct and corroborating sources are pedagogical/tertiary mediators, not the entry's cited monographs (Melchert 2003; Soysal 2004; Klinger 1996), which were not opened this round; Jared Miller's review PDF (entry line 21) failed text extraction, so its passages remain bibliographic only. The 'priest is now speaking in Hattic' gloss and the CTH bilingual numbering are tertiary reports of scholarship, not located tablet readings. The entry's four name-forms Tarḫunna-/Tarḫunt-/Taru/Teššub were only partially spot-checked: Hurrian Teššub and an unnamed Hattic storm-god are confirmed in retrieved text, the exact Hattic 'Taru' and Luwian 'Tarḫunt-' forms were not. Hattic-Caucasian/Yeniseian proposals remain unresolved hypotheses, consistent with (not contradicting) the entry's bad-inference rejection. Wikipedia's Hattian article self-labels parts of the conquest narrative as needing citations; relied on only for the language-classification and ritual-passage statements.

audits.question: Check one dated divine/royal headgear, pointed-cap or horned-crown identification in the entry; distinguish depicted rank, deity/king identification and earlier Hattic or later Neo-Hittite comparators.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/anatolia-hittite.md:120 (horned divine headdress row, 'Not a generic helmet for all human soldiers'), :132 (male divine figures: 'pointed horned headgear'), :123 (Šarruma protects Tudḫaliya IV), :134 (royal rounded-cap row), :46 ('New/Neo-Hittite' terminology trap)
audits.entry_claim: In characteristic imperial representations horned/pointed headgear marks divine status on male deities (short belted garments, pointed horned headgear) and is not a generic human-soldier helmet; royal figures are distinguished within the same visual program (rounded cap; Šarruma embracing Tudḫaliya IV at Yazılıkaya is an explicitly royal late-imperial image); the identification must be tied to a dated image, and Iron Age/'Neo-Hittite' comparators must not be silently projected back into the empire.
audits.source_citation: 'Yazılıkaya', Wikipedia (English), article on the Hittite rock sanctuary near Hattusa, Çorum Province, Turkey.
audits.source_locator: Chamber A procession paragraph; image caption 'Rock carving in Chamber B depicting the god Sharruma and King Tudhaliya IV'
audits.source_excerpt: The left wall shows a procession of male deities, wearing the traditional kilts, pointed shoes and horned hats.
audits.retrieval_method: Direct HTTP fetch of the public Wikipedia article (FetchURL); main extracted text read; quotations copied verbatim. Note: the extractor prefixed a stray first line about the Phrygian Yazılıkaya/Midas City site; the fetched infobox (Çorum Province), body text and captions describe the Hattusa sanctuary and were the only parts used.
audits.basis: Retrieved text locates horned hats specifically on the male-deity procession of Chamber A (rank/status marker inside one documented composition), while the same article identifies the dated Chamber B group as god (Sharruma) and king (Tudhaliya IV) together: 'Rock carving in Chamber B depicting the god Sharruma and King Tudhaliya IV, dated to around 1250–1220 BCE' — deity/king distinction inside one dated 13th-century image, matching entry lines 120/123/132/134. Corroborations date the two chambers to the reigns of Hattusili III (c.1265–c.1240) and Tudhaliya IV (c.1240–c.1215), date further reliefs to the 13th century BCE, document general dating difficulty of Hittite art from lack of inscriptions, and confirm the 'Neo-Hittite' terminology debate that the entry's line-46 trap anticipates. Inspected medium: English tertiary web pages describing the reliefs; no relief plates inspected.
audits.coupling_implication: Supports the entry's role-indexed costume coupling: horned pointed headgear functions as a divine-status marker within a dated composition, distinct from royal headgear in the same sanctuary program, so a design system should index silhouette to role (divine/royal/armed) per dated image rather than to a timeless 'Hittite look'; armed deities and 'god-warrior' royal figures show weapon-bearing and status markers must be read together, not mapped one-to-one onto ethnicity or humanity.
audits.limits: Partial by evidence type: no dated Neo-Hittite horned-cap object was retrieved this round (Livius Karatepe page 404; Smarthistory 403; Met essay 429; UNESCO 403; DAI Hattusa host unresolvable), so the later-comparator separation rests only on the retrieved terminology warning that 'Neo-Hittite' naming is itself debated, not on an Iron Age cap; no earlier Hattic-era headgear comparator was retrieved either. Whether Sharruma's cap in the Tudhaliya IV panel is horned is not stated in the retrieved text, so the specific within-image cap contrast is asserted only for the male-god procession. Sources are tertiary (Wikipedia, Livius, World History Encyclopedia captions); Seeher 2011's plates remain unverified per the entry's own recorded debt; the World History Encyclopedia page fetched as a disambiguation-style page whose usable content is dated image captions.
